blocks.x: It's going now Thomas. Tell me your name. That was Valentine. And what do they call you? Kid Thomas. Kid Thomas huh? Where were you born? Resilient. And when? That was 1860. Some six or something. Well listen, what's the day? The day is January the...
Yeah, it might be January where they are. They ought to be January 12th. Yeah.
January the 27th. Yeah, yeah. 27. I got it on my watch. Yeah, 27, 1969. I just want to get it on there so they'll know who you are. Yeah, sure.
When did you start playing in here, Thomas? I don't know, I was around about 60 years or so.
See? And what was your life like out there in the country as a kid?

Well, I had to work. I had to work. Work in the field, you know what I mean? Work in the sugar refinery, you know what I mean? I do a different kind of job, you know? I do a different thing. I did a different thing. I did a different thing. I did everything, you know?
Mm-hmm.
It was kind of rough, you know what I mean?
Oh, yeah. And tell me something about music. What's your favorite big band? Which one did you like best?
Well, I didn't have no preference but bands, you know what I mean?
You have a favorite musician there? I liked, listen, Armstrong playing, you know?

What was he like, you know, his playing, you know what I mean? A lot of people asked me why, you know what I mean, why I don't play that game. And you know what I mean? You know what I mean? Why don't you play that game? Yeah. You know what I mean? You know what I mean? I don't play that game. I said, well, no. I said, you're not supposed to play. You play your own style, you know? So I always liked his playing. Yeah. Always liked his playing.
And when you started out as a kid, who was your favorite?

Well, let me run it back and see how it's doing. So, dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear
Do you like progressive jazz?
No, I don't like progressive.
Not at all?

No. Well, progressive, I don't like progressive. And they rock and roll. You best, I tell it, I tell you, one music I like the best, it's western, you know, like that, I prefer that kind of music. But they have nice, you know, they have nice numbers, you know. Because I feel, I feel, I used to feel a lot of western songs, when I was playing for dancers, you know. So, boy, they, you know, they came in. I don't like that, I don't understand it, that's why.
Well, tell me about your first recording session that you ever made. Well, I made with Mr. Bill Russell.
Yeah, that's the first one I made. That's the deal.
When Olden and David put up the money. Yeah, I was, I was, yeah. Well, tell me about it, what was it like? It was all right.

You know, people asked me for, a girl like me, they said, you wasn't nice when you first made the regards. I said, no I wasn't. What was you gonna be nice for? First of all, you see, I said, just run into it, they don't know, don't worry about it, you know what I mean? You know, annoying, being nervous to do something. I said, I went on and made it, first, first recording.
You have trouble finding the trombone player?

Robert Thomas was supposed to make the recording, you know, but he had to play that night. But, you know, full on, they let so long, time, you know, and it got late. So finally, well, he had to leave. So, well, I got Hazard Bourne. And Hazard Bourne, he hadn't been on for 16 years. So he's sitting there, I said, I went and the guy told him to go, I'm gonna go get Hazard Bourne. Oh, he said, man, I don't care, I can make it. I said, oh man, you can make it.

He did all pretty good. You know what I mean? He did pretty good. Yeah, he did pretty good. Yeah, he did pretty good. How did you like the rhythm? It was all right. Yeah, it was nice. It was coming all right.

I brought my record over here one day last week for a young lady to listen at it, you know what I mean? He had never, he had me the first, I told him about the first record we had meeting him, I said, I sure would like to hear it, you know. So, there was nothing to that, you know.
Well, would you advise a young man or lady to get into the music business? Sure, I was doing that last night.

I was standing there last night, I said, she told me she had some, a bride, a nephew, you know, he liked this kind of music. So they had three of them. I said, well, all you need three more. He said, well, I'm really working on it, you know what I mean? He said, they got a lot of old jazz records, you know, you know, play them, you know, play them so they can, you know what I mean, get kind of acquainted, you know. So I said, I said, I said, I'm going to stop, don't quit working on it, I keep working on it.
He said, I'm going to stay away on it.
So.
Would you say that New Orleans' music today is the same as it used to be fifty years ago? Well, I'll tell you.

It had quite a change there, you know what I mean? But you see, I'll tell you, years ago when this jazz came down, a lot of fellas didn't play this kind of music. A lot of fellas had big bands, you know. They had big bands. They had big twelve, fourteen piece bands, you see? All them fellas like the old man, you know, Robichaud and Piron and all them fellas, you know, they had great big bands. But this only last year, some of these fellas started playing this kind of music, you know what I mean? But they never did play that kind of music. But you see, my band, our band, we never did quit playing that music. But still, you know, we never did change. And when they come around this jazz business, we played over at the New Orleans Rouge, you see? And we had a lot of offers of people, you know, we should have been the top jazz band in town, because we never stopped playing it, you know what I mean? So a lot of these fellas, they just stopped playing jazz. And the people, when you take the people that come there, the Preservation Hall, a lot of people have told me, they said, I heard these bands play, but a lot of these bands are not together. You know, people sit and listen, you know what I mean? And then they asked me, they said, I know you fellas must have been together many years. I said, oh yeah, we've been together. Of course I've had to lose quite a few members in the band, you know what I mean? I said, but we could tell that you've all been playing together a long time, you know what I mean? But a lot of these fellas, you know what I mean, just started playing this kind of music, and they don't know much about it. They tried to, you know what I mean? They tried to.
They really tried to, I mean. They tried to, you know what I mean. How do you keep your band together? Well, I tell you.

You see, that's a question people ask me too. I never change nobody in my band. I always try to keep the same men. You see, when you have an organization, you keep the same people, you don't have to tell nobody what to do. You know, everybody knows what they have to do. You see? So the only way I change, somebody dies or something like that, you know. But I never change nobody in my band. They never did that. I always keep the same members, you know what I mean? And a lot of fellas, you know, tell me, man, kids, you sure have a lot of patience, you know what I mean? Well, I said, that's what you've got to have, patience. I said, if you don't get somewhere, you know what I mean? I said, you've got to have patience. They go, you sure got better patience. I said, sure, you've got to have what you've got to have. So, I said, a lot of them, you know, and they say, man, I couldn't be like that. I said, I know. I said, that's why a lot of people don't get nowhere either, because they don't get no patience to do things. I said, I've got a lot of patience for that. You know what I mean? Especially trying to keep an organization together, you know what I mean? Of course, they sometimes be a little rough, but you know what I mean? One of these times is a pity, you know what I mean?
Does anybody ever try to stick a special man in your band and get rid of your regular fellas? Like for recording or television or anything? No, no, no.

I'll tell you one thing about most people that came here, you know what I mean? They want to make a recording, but they want to pick a man here, a man there, you know what I mean? And they think that makes a band. That don't make no band, you know what I mean? See? Most of the time people come here. They come to the horn. That's what they do. They want to get a man here, they get a man there, they get a man there, you know what I mean? And that's no good, you know what I mean? But, well, they don't know no band. They think it makes a band. You know, a fella told me, a fella told me in Minneapolis, the last time I was in the band, he said, kid, why is that when the people come to make a recording? They always want you up. They always want maybe to take you, or your band, and take a other fella from some other band, and think, why they don't take your foot band? See, to make a better recording. I said, well, you can't. I said, you think about it, a fella, you can't explain it to some people, they don't know better, you can't explain it to them. Tell them, you know what I mean, that they're wrong, you know what I mean? But they think, that makes a band. But I know they don't make a band, I mean, we don't make no band. So, I thought, well, you have to pick your choice, if you want to make it to me. But I probably don't have to do that in the morning, you know what I mean?
Let me move the mic again. What do you want to do when you retire? When you quit playing music, and quit working days, and everything?

What I want to do, what you going to do? Just sit there and die, that's what you going to do. That's all you going to do, you know what I mean? Once you sit there, that's it. You know what I mean? So, as long as the man can give you the life and help, keep it going, you know what I mean? Just keep going, it's good to be going, you know what I mean? Good to go, you know what I mean? So, that's how I feel about it, you know what I mean? I'm not looking for the hard way, you know what I mean? To do the hard way, you know what I mean? Nothing like that. You know what I mean? So. What do you do now? Well, I've been doing a lot of things for myself, you know what I mean? I have a lot of weight for other people to do too. Right now, I've got a lot of weight definitely to do now, but three or four months to weight there right now. But I don't know. I'm here to get somebody else to do the painting, the house, you know, to paint on the other side, and some rooms inside. I'm here to paint the rooms inside, you know what I mean? And get somebody to paint the outside, you know what I mean? Because I ain't looking for all that weight. So I've been waiting for the people so long, and they don't want nobody else, you see? That's the trouble, you know what I mean? And it'd be too glad to have me there, you know what I mean? So this man, he told me, he said, Thomas, I'd sure be glad to have you, because I know you come and wait for us, we won't have to worry about nothing, you know what I mean? Because you know just what to do. See, when you get a strange fellow, you're going to explain everything, you know what I mean? Probably have to maybe watch him and all that kind of stuff. I'd say, well, that don't go for me, you know what I mean? So I guess I might get him somebody, you know what I mean? To do that, that's a lot of weight. Because we got a lot of weight that would be done, you know what I mean?

What about Roy, that fellow from California, can anybody learn how to play a drum or a horn? What do you mean? Can just anybody off the street learn how to play? You think anybody can learn how to play? Well, I tell you, sometimes a fellow don't have it.

He try hard enough. You know a fellow told me about his kid. That fellow told me about his kid not long ago, you see? He bought a certain drum for his kid. He said, oh, he really tried. You know what I mean? He said he really liked it, but he tried with somebody and he couldn't make it. I said, well, but he gave up too quick. You got to keep at it, you know what I mean? You got to have interesting things when you do things, you know what I mean? See? And you got to do one thing at a time, you know. You can't do three or four things at a time. So you just got to keep right at it, you know what I mean?
Can they learn it at any age?
Huh?
Can they learn it at any age, no matter how young they are, no matter how old?

Sure, they got kids. They got kids learning how to play quite young. Sure. I look at a fellow, a little kid, he said, but look, he sat on the chair, he couldn't put his foot on the floor. And he played a guitar, you know, you know, that kid played a guitar. He was a professor, he was the one who was teaching him, you know. He was a person who was nice to get a guitar, you know. And he was cutting you away with something like that, you know what I mean? A little bit of fingers. So he made it. He grew up now, you know, you ought to play much better now, you know what I mean? But anything you want to take, you got to take a lot of interest in it, you know what I mean? And you're not supposed to, of course it'll disgust you, you know. You get disgusted, you know. But now, some of these people want a lot of plans for them in two, three days. But that's impossible. You never get through that in your music, you know. It can be 90,000 years, you know what I mean? You never get through. But a lot of these kids, they want to learn a dance in two, three days. Now you take notes like the rock and rollers, they don't, they won't, in fact, if they take a couple lessons, all they want to learn a few position on the guitar, and they get in the band. You understand what I mean? But this kind of music, you ain't going to just say, you know, I'm going to learn that in one day or 22 days, you know what I mean? It take a long time to learn, you know what I mean? Sure.
Do you ever get too old to learn?

Well, it all depends. It all depends. It all depends. Now, you take a lot of people, they are, they learn, they take up music, they learn how to play music only just for themselves. They don't want to play out of nowhere, you know what I mean? They take such an energy, they might take a piano, guitar, violin, something like this, you know? And he just want to just entertain his own self, you know what I mean? A lot of people, you know? They don't, they're not particularly playing no band, you know, he just entertain himself, you know? And he's supposed to be a wonderful piano player, you know what I mean? And he goes to talk, you know? She used to play in clubs, but she learned just to play for herself, entertain herself, you know? And different people are hurting. First thing you know, people start hiding, go out and play, you know, in different places, you know what I mean? You go amongst people, then you get a lot of experience amongst people, you know what I mean? But you just sit there, you never get no experience. That's the only way you get experience, going around with different people, you know what I mean? Different conversation, you know what I mean? She said, yeah, that's a good idea. I said, sure, I know it's a good idea.
Well when you started off, did you have a real horn or did you make your own horn?

No, I had a. When we first started playing, we made some instruments, you know? Or a reed, canned reed, you know? And we made a bass with some fishing rod, you know? And we had a little club, you know? We made a club, me and Ed, Robert Hall, Ed, and all the brothers, you know? And different other fellas got together and things like that, you know? So finally, well, you know, well, their daddy was a clarinet player. Well they wanted to learn how to play clarinet. So what we did, we bought a clarinet, ten dollars. So Robert, yeah, Robert, he learned on the clarinet. Then Edmund learned on the clarinet. Then Hayward, or Calvin, he learned on the clarinet. Three of them. And the other one, the other one after one, he comes to the youngies. He's coming after and he's going to have to play. Herb, is he? Herb. Yeah, the one in New York. And the other one in the country where he picked up playing a bass on. He played in bands, the boys had a band out there, you know, a big band out there in the country, Susaphone. But well, I was playing around with them, you know what I mean? We couldn't play anymore, when we did start from the entrance, we couldn't play anymore about three songs, you know. We played all night, you know, three songs, playing slow this night, make time fast, you know what I mean? And the people liked it. So this man had a clubhouse, his wife followed. He was kicking on me. We couldn't play anymore than three songs. How many keys? We ain't no one key, that's all we know. You know what I mean? But we used to take one number at a time, you know what I mean? Until you get that, that's what you got to do with music, you know. So he played that, then after that, oh, we're beginning to get really good then. So the brother, he built a pavilion, really dance all day, you know. Oh well he was getting good then. Then after we started getting good, you know what we did, we brought a whole fellow out there who had a bar, well he's rich. We went to him and we sat down and explained to him what we had to do for us. He said yeah. So we stood for the influence for us. We got to make a room all, a whole set. It was a whole of them. It was a whole of them. We got to do the whole set and we played for this fellow. And the half time we started playing different places. Play on this side of the river, play on the other side of the river, you know what I mean? All of them down the river, you know what I mean? So, yeah. Did you like to work in the fields out there? No, I never did like to work. I never did like to work. I don't like to work. I never do work, you know what I mean, but I don't like it, you know what I mean? Oh yeah, I'll tell you the truth. I did a little bit of everything. I did a little bit of everything. I worked in a railroad shop. I worked on the railroad and rolled concrete. Sometimes building bridges and culverts, you know, tap all over culverts, put concrete, and once you start building bridges, you know, you know, you know, you know, you know, you can't stop, you see. You got to finish it because it's a setup, you see. Sometimes we'll be in the water up to here, to our neck. Well, yeah. I mean the cold water too, in the wintertime. And so, well, then I got this job in a railroad shop, right there. And after depression came, so I'm getting a little bit of a little bit of a little bit to build power to build power to build power to build power to build power to build power to build power to build power to build power to build power to build power to build power to build power to build power to build power to build power to build power to build power to build power to build power to build power to build power to build power to build power
to build power to build power to build power to build power to build power to build power to

I started painting for them in time of depression. So finally I painted for him and I painted for another part of this painting from Wonder Garden and all down there. And this kept me going. So after that, when the wall broke down, and I came back and I got a job, I come back in a railroad shop. So I've always been down the wall like that. And after the shop closed on, they moved away and out of there, I went there. But I didn't like that because it was too much hard to wait there for me. So they laid me off. But what I did, I went back to the lawns, you know, wait for them.

Well tell me about it. The last time you ever worked in the fields out in the country, your last day, what was that like? Well, I don't know, let me see. The last time I was awake. I think your daddy told me about this.
Yeah. I can't remember now the last time.

Well, just that he told me that you went out there and, uh, you laid the hole down and never came back. He left. Right, right. Didn't get you pay or anything. Never. But anyway, uh, I wanted to ask you about, uh, that clarinet player from out of the country that quit playing. You know the man I'm talking about? Oh yeah.

I was playing with that band. After all these boys left from there, I went to play with that band. You know what I mean? Oh yeah, you're talking about, uh, well he got a French name. Lili. That's his name. That's all I know his name, Lili. He was a good boy, you know that boy was a nice, class day. And after I was down, I got him to come play with, uh, yeah, when I first came down here, I played with Mud Carey's brother, you know, and, uh, I got him to come here to, uh, Jack Carey, you know, to play down here with them, with us, you know what I mean? But somewhere, I don't know what happened with that clan that's playing, something happened and the man just quit playing it, you know what I mean? Real quit playing it. And me and that boy, we were just like two brothers, you know what I mean? Oh, I played that band a long time. And most all of them fellas in that band done died of. Was he good? Yeah, he was a good player. Boy, now that man would have been famous, you know what I mean? But something, I don't know, I don't know what happened, I'm going to tell you the truth. I don't know what happened.
He wouldn't fool the clan anymore. Was he as good as Edmund Hall?

Oh no, no, he wasn't good at him. No, no, he wasn't good at him, but he could play, you know what I mean? Now Edmund, not that but Edmund. Now Edmund is a fella, look, in all the clan that played, he's the only fella picked up a clan that just went on and played. You know what I mean? They didn't do it for the only clan that I mean. Funny thing about it, it just was a gift, you know what I mean? It just was a gift, that's right. It didn't take him all them years to play that clan, right? Because after he got there, picked that clan that was playing, it began to get good there at home. So he left and he came here, you see? Played the band here. And after that he left and he went to New York. Well he didn't take him long to learn that kind of thing. Did you ever play on the levee? Yeah, on the levee. We used to throw on the levee. We'd go play for dancing, we'd throw on the levee. Sometimes we'd come home early from the job, we'd get four in the morning, four o'clock, four o'clock, five o'clock in the morning, we'd get on the levee and throw on the levee. And man music traveled, everything nice and quiet you know. Oh yeah, we used to do it often. Oh most of the time we'd go play, play on the dances. We'd have to play on the porch, like the halls you know, have a porch, you have to play out there, or you'd get on the levee and play for the, you know what I mean? Sure, I did that since I've been here, you know where we'd go to the country and play. Sure. Oh yeah, we did a lot at the same time. Sure. We did a lot at the same time. We'd come home early from the job, we'd get four in the morning, four o'clock, four o'clock in the morning, we'd get on the levee and play on the levee. And man music traveled, everything nice and quiet, you know. And then we'd get on the levee and play on the levee and play for the, you know what I mean? Sure, I did that since I've been here, you know where we'd go to country and play. Sure. Oh yeah, we did a lot at the same time. Did you have a drink, Thomas? Well I never was a drinker. I have, you know what I mean, I might sometimes take a little highball or maybe a beer or something, but it just don't agree with me, so I don't fool you. You know what I mean? I don't care about it. And I'm glad too. I'm really glad. He ain't missing nothing. He ain't missing a thing. Because me and Father lick a head out, you know what I mean, I'd been ruined. So I just, in fact a lot of people think I drink, you know what I mean? You know what I tell them? I say every time I come on the job I'm drunk. You know what I mean? Every time I come on the job I'm drunk. They think I drink, but I'm drunk. I ain't drink a can of beer, I'm telling you the truth. I usually drink a little beer. And I, you know, I ain't drink a can of beer enough going maybe but a year now.
I just don't care about it, you know what I mean?

I just don't care about it. I have liquor at home then, what you call, gave me a bottle of champagne, man. A really genuine champagne. Gave me that for going with praise when I was going in there. And you know I still got that bottle of champagne in there. Tell somebody to come in and drink it. I'm drinking.
Yeah I know.

Sure. But I just don't, you know what I mean. I don't, you know. A lot of people, you see I tell it to a lot of people, a lot of people think, if you say you're drinking, they think you think you're sick more than anybody. No, no, you don't think you're sick more than anybody. You know what I mean? What be useful in something where you don't agree with you and make you sick? You know what I mean? That's why I used to, look, that's why I quit drinking coffee. Used to give me a lot of gas. And I just quit drinking. A lot of people say you just imagine that. But no, I didn't imagine it. I didn't imagine that. So I don't think nothing was going on with me. No, no. I would drink a little Coca-Cola or something like that, a little lemonade or something like that, you know what I mean? No, I didn't mean I'd do that, you know what I mean? I went out to Japan, three months, I said everywhere you would go, they had tea and coffee. And I thought it was funny, I couldn't sleep at night, you know? So when I came back, me and I was talking, me and Paul was talking about, he asked me how we met him. Paul said, man, tea keeps you from sleeping. I said, I thought there was something wrong. He said, keep you from sleeping too much. And everywhere we'd go, it would be tea and coffee, you know what I mean? Man, I couldn't rest. I couldn't sleep the same one like that way late in, way late hours, you know what I mean? So I don't fool nothing was going on with me, you know what I mean? If you don't fool with something, you know something don't agree with you, if you don't fool with it, you'll last a long time and never complain too much, you know what I mean? But what they used, I don't know. I just don't do it, that's all. I like all that now, I'm going to remember, I ain't going to think I don't like no coffee, I really love it, you know, because I really love it, you know what I mean? I'm thinking of it against me now, so they used to be fooling.
Tell me something, how come you sing so high when you sing milk cow blues?
High?
Yeah, you sing like that?
Well I didn't change my boy.
Why do you do that?

I didn't do it for kicks. Yeah, kicks, I didn't do it for kicks, man. You know what I mean? People like that, you know what I mean? You know a lot of people think that we like and sing here. Well man, I wish I could sing. Man, who? No, but I didn't do it for kicks, that's all. You know, the people get a kick out of it, you know what I mean? They don't play my first days, you know what I mean? Man, you can play, play me a cow blues for it. See, we like the way you, you know what I mean? We like the way you sing there, you know what I mean? I didn't do it for kicks. A lot of things I do for kicks, you know what I mean? People like it, you know. Yeah, most of what it folks, you know what I mean?
Did you ever see any big crowds in New Orleans?
How do you mean crowds? Sure.
A crowd of people had a place, I mean, like, while you'd be playing. Well there's music here. Oh yeah, sure. What's the biggest crowd you ever played for?

Oh, man, sure. I can't tell you, so many crowds I'd have played for. When I was playing at the Moon Rouge, that was a great big building. You know what I mean? That place you couldn't get in. You know what I mean? Oh yeah, sure. That's right. Oh yeah, there were many people who used to come there. You couldn't get in that place. Sure. Well, now you take at the Preservation Hall. When we first started playing at the Preservation Hall, you know, I'm the first one to start there and I'm the first one to get the man I did to run this. You know what I mean? So, you know how many people we put in that place? One thousand five hundred. You never did have, had red eggs. You know what I mean? Because they used to just check every person, you know, come in, you know what I mean? That's right. Sure. What about lawn parties? What was a lawn party?
Well, a lawn party was this. People used to get a lawn party in the yard, you know what I mean?

Yards, you know. Like some people had a backyard, you know. Well I used to play parties in the Kretna. Used to have three or four parties like tonight, Monday night, you know what I mean? You know what I mean? It was in the rain. All they wanted the rain was to stop falling. That wouldn't stop them from coming out, you know what I mean? I played lawn parties over here for white, for colored, and the other ones. All down below the cut-offs played parties down there, you know what I mean? on the ground, naked ground, you know what I mean? And things like that. Don't care how much rain would fall, the people would come up right on. And when they get too dead, they're going to be dry this floor here. They didn't know that much, you know what I mean? Shut up. I always played a lot of parties, you know what I mean? It was nice, you know what I mean? Them days when, you know, we used to give all these parties. Well, you had different entertainers to go, now you don't have nowhere to go. You don't have nowhere to go.
Yeah, that's the end of the tape, so I don't think we don't have anywhere to go, but back it up and listen to it. Yeah, yeah. So thank you a million, Thomas. We'll be back it up.

segments.title: Tape opening: name, birthplace and date
segments.summary: Interviewer identifies Kid Thomas, his birthplace and the date, January 27, 1969.

segments.title: Rural boyhood: fieldwork and the sugar refinery
segments.summary: Thomas describes a rough country childhood working in the fields and the sugar refinery.

segments.title: Favorite musicians and Armstrong's playing
segments.summary: Thomas has no band preference but always liked Armstrong, and says each player should keep his own style.

segments.title: Dislike of progressive jazz and rock and roll
segments.summary: He does not like progressive jazz or rock and roll and prefers western music, which he played for dancers.

segments.title: First recording session with Bill Russell
segments.summary: He recalls his first record for Bill Russell, financed by Alden and David, and the substitute trombonist after Robert Thomas could not come.

segments.title: Advice to young people entering music
segments.summary: He encourages a young listener's relatives to keep working at jazz and to play old records.

segments.title: New Orleans music then and now; his band never changed style
segments.summary: Big bands once dominated, but his band kept playing the old jazz, so he says it should have been the top band in town.

segments.title: Keeping the same band members together
segments.summary: He keeps the same men and changes only when someone dies, and says patience is the key.

segments.title: Why picking players from different bands does not make a band
segments.summary: Record makers want to mix men from various bands, but he says that does not make a real band.

segments.title: Plans for retirement and work around the house
segments.summary: He says he will keep going rather than sit down, and talks about getting people to paint his house.

segments.title: Can anyone learn music, and at what age
segments.summary: He says learning takes patience and years of interest, can start young, and rock players learn too quickly.

segments.title: Homemade instruments and the Hall brothers' first band
segments.summary: Boys made reed instruments and a fishing-rod bass, the Hall brothers learned clarinet, and the band played dances up and down the river.

segments.title: Railroad shop, bridge work and painting during the Depression
segments.summary: He describes other jobs: railroad shop, concrete bridge work, and painting during the Depression.

segments.title: Last day working in the fields
segments.summary: He cannot recall his last day in the fields; the interviewer says his father said he left without his pay.

segments.title: Clarinetists Lili and Edmond Hall; levee dances and not drinking
segments.summary: He recalls the clarinetist Lili, who quit playing, and says Edmond Hall had a gift and rose quickly. The same block continues with playing dances on the porch and levee and his never being a drinker.

segments.title: Not drinking; tea and coffee on the Japan trip
segments.summary: He says he never drank much and quit coffee, and recalls sleeplessness from tea and coffee in Japan.

segments.title: Singing Milk Cow Blues
segments.summary: Asked why he sings high on Milk Cow Blues, he says he did not do it for kicks and that people like it.

segments.title: Biggest crowds: the Moulin Rouge and Preservation Hall
segments.summary: He recalls packed crowds at the Moulin Rouge and about 1,500 people at Preservation Hall.

segments.title: Lawn parties and closing of the tape
segments.summary: He explains lawn parties in yards and Gretna, played for white and Black crowds in any weather; the tape then ends.
